# Introduction

Alpine ecosystems are among the most vulnerable to climate change [@IPCCSR2019HM]. Resurveys across mountain regions have documented upslope range shifts, increasing summit species richness, and changes in the composition of high-elevation vegetation [@Gottfried2012NatClimChange; @Rumpf2018PNAS; @Lamprecht2018NewPhytol], and rising plant extinction rates on European summits [@Wessely2026Science], while satellite observations show widespread greening of alpine landscapes, concentrated in late-melting snowfields [@Choler2025NatClimChange]. Much of this change reflects the expansion of species that gain a competitive advantage as environmental constraints relax. Examples include woody shrub expansion in Arctic and alpine tundra [@MyersSmith2011ERL; @Bjorkman2018Nature] and the encroachment of grasses and tall forbs into snowbed communities as the snow-free season lengthens [@Grabherr2003book; @Dullinger2003AAA]. In Japanese alpine ecosystems, dwarf bamboo (*Sasa* spp., hereafter *Sasa*) represents a prominent example. *Sasa* forms dense evergreen stands that exclude subordinate species, and its expansion into snowbed meadows has been associated with earlier snowmelt and reductions in plant species richness [@Kudo2011EcoEvo]. Snowbed vegetation has recovered following experimental removal of *Sasa* [@Kudo2017AlpBot]. Understanding where and how rapidly *Sasa* expands is therefore directly relevant to alpine plant conservation.

Snowmelt timing is a central environmental factor for alpine vegetation because it determines the onset and duration of the growing season and is closely linked to growing conditions such as soil temperature and moisture [@Wipf2010PolarRes; @Wahren2005GCB; @Choler2025NatClimChange]; snowmelt date is therefore a proxy for a set of covarying conditions rather than a single driver. Spatial scale matters here. Snowmelt varies with microtopography over distances of less than one to tens of metres, and alpine vegetation forms a fine mosaic of communities along these snowmelt gradients [@KudoIto1992Vegetatio]. Linking changes in alpine plant distributions to environmental conditions therefore requires simultaneous observations of vegetation and snowmelt at approximately 1 m resolution, and the spatial resolution of snow-cover observations strongly conditions what such analyses can detect [@Dedieu2016RemSens]. Field plots capture this scale but lack continuous spatial coverage. Satellites provide decades of snow and vegetation observations at 10–30 m resolution [@BarrouDumont2025TC; @Bayle2025SciData], but cannot resolve community mosaics or movements of patch boundaries. Ground-based time-lapse cameras fill this gap. Repeated daily photographs from a fixed viewpoint allow automated extraction of both per-pixel snowmelt dates and vegetation maps at sub-metre ground resolution [@IdeOguma2013EcolInfom; @Okamoto2024RSEC]. The two approaches are therefore complementary: the expansion patterns that satellites record over decades and at scales of tens of metres can be examined through observations of the metre-scale processes that underlie them.

*Sasa* expands through two contrasting dispersal processes [@Suyama2000MolEcol; @Kudo2011EcoEvo]. The first is the gradual advance of patch fronts through rhizome elongation; where this process dominates, expansion may be limited by the rate of dispersal rather than by the extent of environmentally suitable habitat. The second is establishment from seeds following mass or partial flowering [@Miyazaki2009JPlantRes; @Mizuki2014PLOS], which can bypass local distance constraints and form new patches. Conservation planning requires information on both: where environmental conditions permit *Sasa* to establish if seeds arrive, and how far existing fronts can actually reach. For the former question, habitat suitability models, statistical frameworks relating species presence to environmental conditions, have been widely used in conservation planning and projections of distributional change [@Guisan1998JVS; @Thomas2004Nature; @Gallien2010DD; @Araujo2019SciAdv; @Zurell2020Ecography; @Amagai2022AVS]. Projecting suitability maps without accounting for dispersal constraints, however, can greatly overestimate establishment area [@Engler2009DD; @Engler2012Ecography]. Answering the latter question requires distribution maps of the same area at two or more times: comparing them reveals the cells in which establishment actually occurred. This observed establishment can then be modelled directly as a function of environment and distance from the existing front, projecting expansion as a process rather than as a reassessment of a static suitability map.

Here, we examine *Sasa* expansion on the western slope of Mt. Tateyama in the northern Japanese Alps, where plot resurveys on the Murodo-daira plateau have documented 44–260% expansion of *Sasa* patches over 38 years [@Yoshida2016SasaTateyama]. Using 10 years of time-lapse imagery, we mapped the *Sasa* distribution in 2012 and 2021 and the snowmelt pattern of every 1 m cell, and addressed two questions of direct relevance to the conservation of snowbed vegetation. First, is the observed expansion of *Sasa* associated mainly with environmental conditions, in particular snowmelt timing, or is it limited by the distance over which rhizomes advance from existing patches? Second, if the expansion process of the past decade continues, where, and into which alpine plant communities, is *Sasa* most likely to establish by 2030? To answer these questions, we compared a habitat suitability model of environmental potential (Model A) with a model of observed establishment that accounts for distance from existing patches (Model B), and projected establishment to 2030 by applying the establishment model year by year under explicit snowmelt scenarios.
